beats.headline: Why does your DB pool keep crashing?
beats.subline: It isn't just bad luck. It's usually a leaked connection or a missing try-with-resources.
beats.narration: Most devs treat JDBC like a black box. But when your service throws a connection pool error, you need to know exactly how the driver talks to the database wire.

beats.title: The JDBC Execution Path
beats.subtitle: From Java Service to Database Wire
beats.narration: The flow is simple: borrow from the pool, prepare the statement, bind parameters, and stream the result. If you don't close these in reverse order, you leak resources.

beats.title: The Essential Try-With-Resources

steps.explanation: Ensures the connection returns to the pool even if an exception occurs.
Strict LIFO closing order prevents memory leaks.

beats.narration: Never manually close connections in a finally block. Use try-with-resources. It guarantees that the ResultSet, Statement, and Connection close in the correct order, every time.

beats.title: SQL Injection vs. Parameterization

top.label: Vulnerable
top.code: stmt.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'");

beats.narration: Never concatenate strings. PreparedStatement sends the SQL template first, then the data. The database treats your input as literal text, not executable code. It's the only way to stay safe.

takeaways: Always use column labels in ResultSet

beats.headline: Why is your SQL NULL becoming a zero?
beats.subline: JDBC primitives have no concept of null. Here is how to fix your data integrity.
beats.narration: Calling getInt on a SQL NULL returns zero. That's a silent data bug. Let's fix your mapping logic before it corrupts your production database.

beats.title: Safe Null Handling

steps.explanation: The manual check for primitive nullability.
The modern, clean way to map nullable types.

beats.narration: Stop using raw primitives for nullable columns. Use getObject with the wrapper class. It handles the null check internally and keeps your domain models clean.

beats.title: The RowMapper Abstraction

steps.explanation: Decouples query execution from object mapping.
Allows passing a lambda for every query.

beats.narration: Extracting a RowMapper interface is the secret to readable code. It separates the 'how to fetch' from the 'how to map', making your DAOs testable and DRY.

beats.title: Memory Safety: Buffering vs. Streaming
beats.narration: Loading 2 million rows into memory will crash your JVM. To stream, you must disable auto-commit and set a fetch size. The driver then pulls rows in chunks.

beats.headline: Is your pool size actually hurting performance?
beats.subline: More connections don't mean more speed. Here is the math for optimal pool sizing.
beats.narration: Most devs set their pool size to 100 and wonder why latency spikes. Oversized pools cause context switching and lock contention. Let's calculate the real number.

beats.title: ConcurrentBag Borrow Path
beats.subtitle: How HikariCP avoids global locks
beats.narration: HikariCP uses ConcurrentBag. It checks your thread's local cache first, then does a lock-free scan. It's designed to stay fast even under heavy contention.

beats.title: The Golden Sizing Formula
beats.caption: Baseline for Postgres/MySQL

lines.text: ✗ Don't match pool size to web threads!

beats.narration: The formula is simple: cores times two plus disks. If you have 8 replicas, your pool size should be tiny. Oversized pools just fight over the same CPU cores.

beats.title: Detecting Connection Leaks
beats.code:
config.setLeakDetectionThreshold(5000);
// Logs stack trace if borrowed > 5s

steps.explanation: Warns you when a connection is held too long.

beats.narration: Enable leak detection in production. If a connection is held for more than 5 seconds, Hikari logs the exact line of code that leaked it. It's a lifesaver.

beats.headline: Why are your bulk inserts taking forever?
beats.subline: Network round-trips are the silent killer. Batching is the cure.
beats.narration: Executing 10,000 inserts in a loop is a network disaster. Batching turns 10,000 round-trips into a handful of packets. Let's optimize your throughput.

beats.title: Efficient Batching

steps.explanation: Flushes to the DB in one round-trip.

beats.narration: Batching is key. Use a batch size like 500 and flush regularly. Pair this with the driver's rewrite flag in your JDBC URL to get maximum performance.

beats.title: The Rewrite Flag
beats.caption: Essential for bulk inserts
beats.narration: This flag is magic. It rewrites your batched statements into multi-row inserts, cutting your ingestion time by an order of magnitude.

beats.title: JDBC Checklist
beats.narration: Stop using legacy patterns. Modern JDBC is fast, safe, and reliable if you follow these rules. Your database will thank you for the reduced load.
